title: Encoding vs Hashing vs Encryption
summary: Three things often mixed up, with very different goals.

pages.title: Encoding: a format change, not a secret
pages.body:
Encoding converts data to another format so it can be sent or stored safely in a technical sense. Examples: Base64, URL encoding, and hex.

Key point: encoding uses no key. Anyone can reverse it. "Q0lQSEVS" is just the Base64 of "CIPHER".

So if an app "secures" passwords with Base64, they aren't secured at all.
pages.tip: Encoding is like translating text to Morse code. Not a secret, just a different form.

pages.title: Hashing: a one-way fingerprint
pages.body:
A hash turns any data into a fixed-length string, e.g. SHA-256 is always 64 hex characters.

Properties:
- One-way: it can't be reversed into the original data
- Change one letter and the result changes completely
- The same data always gives the same hash

Used to store passwords and to check files haven't changed (download checksums).
pages.tip: A hash is a fingerprint. You can take a print from a finger, but you can't rebuild the finger from the print.

pages.title: Encryption: secrets with a key
pages.body:
Encryption scrambles data with a key, and only someone with the key can restore it (decryption).

Compared with the other two:
- Encoding: reversible by anyone, no key
- Hashing: not reversible at all
- Encryption: reversible, but only with the key

Examples: WhatsApp end-to-end chats, HTTPS, and phone storage encryption.
pages.tip: Encryption is a safe. You can get the contents back, but only with the key.

quiz.prompt: Base64 is...
quiz.explanation: Base64 only changes the format; anyone can reverse it without a key.

quiz.prompt: The main property of a hash is...
quiz.explanation: Hashes are designed to be one-way and consistent for the same input.

quiz.prompt: Which is reversible, but only with a key?
quiz.explanation: Encryption needs a key to decrypt.

quiz.prompt: An app stores passwords in Base64. This is...
quiz.explanation: Encoding isn't protection. Passwords must be hashed with a dedicated algorithm.

quiz.prompt: A SHA-256 checksum on a download page is used to...
options: Verify the file wasn't altered or corrupted
quiz.explanation: If your downloaded file's hash matches the listed one, the contents are identical.

title: Classic Ciphers
summary: Caesar and Vigenère: how they work, and why they're easy to break today.

pages.title: The Caesar cipher
pages.body:
One of the oldest ciphers. Every letter shifts a fixed number of places. With a shift of 3: A→D, B→E, ... X→A.

"HELLO" becomes "KHOOR".

Its weakness: there are only 25 possible shifts. A computer, or even a patient human, can try them all in seconds. This is called brute force.
pages.tip: Caesar is a one-digit combination lock. At most 25 tries and it opens.

pages.title: Vigenère: shifting shifts
pages.body:
Vigenère uses a keyword. Each key letter sets the shift for the matching message letter. The key "KEY" means shift 10, 4, 24, then repeat.

That way the same letter doesn't always become the same letter, making it harder to guess. For centuries it was called "the unbreakable cipher".

But because the key repeats, patterns can still be analyzed, and computers now break it easily.
pages.tip: Vigenère is a lock whose combination changes every letter, but the combinations cycle in the same order forever.

pages.title: Frequency analysis
pages.body:
In every language, some letters appear far more often. In English, E is the most common; in Indonesian, A.

Classic ciphers only shuffle letters; they don't hide these patterns. So if R is the most common letter in a ciphertext, it's probably a disguised E or A.

The lesson: never invent your own encryption for real data. Use modern, tested algorithms like AES.

Try it yourself in Toolbox → Cipher.
pages.tip: A disguise changes the clothes, not the walk: people who know you can still guess.

quiz.prompt: With a Caesar shift of 3, the letter A becomes...
quiz.explanation: A shifted three places: B, C, D.

quiz.prompt: Why is Caesar easy to break?
quiz.explanation: Every possibility can be tried quickly (brute force).

quiz.prompt: Vigenère sets each letter's shift based on...
quiz.explanation: Each keyword letter gives a different, repeating shift.

quiz.prompt: Frequency analysis exploits...
quiz.explanation: Classic ciphers don't hide letter frequency patterns.

quiz.prompt: To encrypt real data you should...
options: Use a modern, tested algorithm like AES
quiz.explanation: Homemade algorithms almost always have hidden weaknesses.

title: Hashing & Password Storage
summary: Salts, slow algorithms, and why MD5 is retired.

pages.title: A good server doesn't know your password
pages.body:
A properly built app doesn't store your actual password. It stores the hash. At login, what you type is hashed again and compared.

If the database leaks, attackers get hashes, not passwords. But they can still guess: hash common words, then match.

Precomputed tables of hashes for this kind of guessing are called rainbow tables.
pages.tip: A good guard doesn't keep a copy of your house key, only a photo of its shape to compare against.

pages.title: Salt: a unique seasoning per user
pages.body:
A salt is random, unique data added to a password before hashing, then stored alongside the hash.

Benefits:
- Two people with the same password get different hashes
- Rainbow tables become useless, since they'd have to be rebuilt per salt

A salt isn't secret. Its job is to make mass guessing expensive.
pages.tip: Two identical bowls of soup taste different because each gets a different secret seasoning.

pages.title: Why it must be slow
pages.body:
MD5 and SHA-1 were designed to be fast. Great for checksums, bad for passwords, because computers can guess billions of times per second. MD5 is also considered broken.

For passwords, use deliberately slow algorithms with a tunable cost:
- bcrypt
- scrypt
- Argon2 (the modern recommendation)

For users: since leaks still happen, a long, unique password per account remains the key defense.
pages.tip: A door that takes one second to open doesn't bother the owner, but frustrates a thief trying a million keys.

quiz.prompt: A secure app stores passwords as...
quiz.explanation: Salted hashes keep the real password unstored and hard to mass-guess.

quiz.prompt: A salt's purpose is to...
options: Make hashes unique even for identical passwords
quiz.explanation: A random salt makes rainbow tables useless.

quiz.prompt: A rainbow table is...
options: A precomputed set of hashes for guessing passwords
quiz.explanation: A table of hashes for many commonly used passwords.

quiz.prompt: Why is MD5 unsuitable for passwords?
quiz.explanation: Fast algorithms let attackers guess billions of times per second.

quiz.prompt: The currently recommended password hashing algorithm is...
quiz.explanation: Argon2 is deliberately slow and memory-hard, making mass guessing costly.

title: Symmetric & Asymmetric Keys
summary: One shared key vs a public-private key pair.

pages.title: Symmetric: one shared key
pages.body:
In symmetric encryption, the same key locks and unlocks. Example: AES.

It's fast and great for large data. The problem: how do you send the key to the other person without it being intercepted? If the key travels the same channel, an eavesdropper gets it too.
pages.tip: Like one padlock key with a duplicate. Handy, but getting the duplicate to a distant friend is the hard part.

pages.title: Asymmetric: public and private keys
pages.body:
Asymmetric encryption uses a linked pair of keys:
- Public key: can be shared with anyone
- Private key: kept to yourself, must never leak

A message locked with the public key can only be opened by its matching private key. So anyone can send you a secret message without exchanging keys first. Examples: RSA and elliptic curves (ECC).
pages.tip: A public key is a mailbox with a slot. Anyone can drop in a letter, but only the key holder can open the box.

pages.title: Used together
pages.body:
Asymmetric is safe for exchanging keys but slow. Symmetric is fast but hard to share. The answer: combine them.

- Use asymmetric to agree on or send a symmetric key safely
- Then encrypt all data with that symmetric key

This pattern powers HTTPS, WhatsApp, and VPNs. Private keys are also used for digital signatures, covered in the next module.
pages.tip: Send the safe's key through a secure mailbox, then keep everything in the fast-opening safe.

quiz.prompt: Symmetric encryption means...
options: The same key locks and unlocks
quiz.explanation: AES is symmetric: one shared key.

quiz.prompt: The key that can be shared with anyone is the...
quiz.explanation: Public keys are made to be shared.

quiz.prompt: A message is locked with Nadia's public key. Who can open it?
options: Only the holder of Nadia's private key
quiz.explanation: Only the matching private key can open it.

quiz.prompt: The main problem with symmetric encryption is...
quiz.explanation: The key must reach the recipient without interception.

quiz.prompt: HTTPS uses...
quiz.explanation: Asymmetric for the key, symmetric for the data because it's faster.

title: HTTPS, Certificates & Signatures
summary: How browsers know a site is real, and what the padlock means.

pages.title: Digital signatures
pages.body:
A private key can also "sign" data. Anyone can verify the signature with the public key.

A digital signature proves two things:
- Authenticity: the data really came from the private key's owner
- Integrity: the data hasn't changed since it was signed

A real example: Android app updates are signed by the developer. If the signature differs, the phone refuses to install it over the old app.
pages.tip: A digital signature is a wax seal with a personal stamp: anyone can check it's genuine, but only the stamp's owner can make it.

pages.title: Certificates and Certificate Authorities
pages.body:
When you open an HTTPS site, the server sends a certificate containing its public key and domain name. The certificate is signed by a Certificate Authority (CA), an organization trusted by browsers and operating systems.

The browser checks:
- The CA signature is valid
- The domain name matches
- The certificate hasn't expired

If anything fails, a red warning appears. That's why certificate warnings must never be skipped.
pages.tip: A certificate is a site's ID card; the CA is the government office. The browser trusts the ID because it trusts the issuer.

pages.title: What the padlock really means
pages.body:
The padlock in the address bar means your connection to that server is encrypted and the server really controls that domain.

But a padlock doesn't mean the site is honest. Scammers can get free certificates for fake domains like bank-official-prize.com. The connection is secure, but you're still talking to a scammer.

So always check the domain name carefully, not just the padlock.
pages.tip: The padlock guarantees your letter stays sealed on the way. But if the address is wrong, the sealed letter still reaches the wrong person.

quiz.prompt: A digital signature proves...
options: The sender is authentic and the data unchanged
quiz.explanation: Signatures guarantee authenticity and integrity.

quiz.prompt: Why can't an APK with a different signature replace the old app?
options: Android ensures updates come from the same developer
quiz.explanation: A different signature could mean a fake app, so Android refuses it.

quiz.prompt: A Certificate Authority (CA)...
quiz.explanation: Browsers trust certificates because a trusted CA signed them.

quiz.prompt: A scam site has an HTTPS padlock. This means...
options: The connection is encrypted, but it can still be a scam
quiz.explanation: The padlock covers the connection, not the owner's honesty.

quiz.prompt: Your browser warns the domain doesn't match the certificate. You should...
options: Not continue and not enter any data
Post a screenshot to a group
quiz.explanation: It's a sign of a fake site or an intercepted connection.
